name: 6th ABAW Competition
description: This paper describes the 6th Affective Behavior Analysis in-the-wild (ABAW) Competition, which is part of the respective Workshop held in conjunction with IEEE CVPR 2024. The 6th ABAW Competition addresses contemporary challenges in understanding human emotions and behaviors, crucial for the development of human-centered technologies. In more detail, the Competition focuses on affect related benchmarking tasks and comprises of five sub-challenges: i) Valence-Arousal Estimation (the target is to estimate two continuous affect dimensions, valence and arousal), ii) Expression Recognition (the target is to recognise between the mutually exclusive classes of the 7 basic expressions and 'other'), iii) Action Unit Detection (the target is to detect 12 action units), iv) Compound Expression Recognition (the target is to recognise between the 7 mutually exclusive compound expression classes), and v) Emotional Mimicry Intensity Estimation (the target is to estimate six continuous emotion dimensions). In the paper, we present these Challenges, describe their respective datasets and challenge protocols (we outline the evaluation metrics) and present the baseline systems as well as their obtained performance. More information for the Competition can be found in: https://affective-behavior-analysis-in-the-wild.github.io/6th.
evaluation_method: Task-specific metrics (Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) for valence/arousal and intensity; F1 / accuracy for expression and AU detection)
general_score_metric: Task-specific (primary metrics include CCC for VA/intensity and F1/accuracy for classification/AU tasks)
typical_sota_score: Valence-Arousal (CCC) ~0.4–0.6; Expression Recognition accuracy ~50–75%; Action Unit detection F1 ~40–65%; Compound expression recognition ~40–65%; Emotional Mimicry intensity (CCC) ~0.2–0.5
reputation: A well-established, annual competition in affective computing that is widely recognized in the community for in-the-wild affect benchmarking.
notes: Multi-task benchmark with different metrics per sub-challenge; in-the-wild data with annotation noise and class imbalance; non-LLM benchmark focused on vision/affective computing.
